title: Stream Synchronizer and Attention Slice Regulator
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Our serving runtime shows occasional p99 tail spikes for streaming responses when heterogeneous request sizes interact with kernel selection and prefill scheduling. Root causes observed in production traces: small bursts of short-sequence requests cause repeated kernel handoffs and fragmented attention prefetches; long continuations compete for KV cache slots; admission gating is too permissive for mixed-priority tenants.

Goal: Reduce streaming p99 by 30% (baseline: 220ms) and p95 by 15% for mixed workloads without increasing median latency by more than 5ms. Deliver a coordinated feature that: 1) introduces a stream synchronizer to align short streams into micro-windows for kernel reuse, 2) adds an attention slice regulator to pre-warm attention and KV caches based on predicted continuation, and 3) improves admission pacing heuristics to limit tail amplification during microbursts.

Why this is different: Rather than only widening batching windows or hard throttles, this approach shapes the input stream (lightweight coalescing) and optimizes attention prefetching so kernel selection has higher affinity across adjacent micro-batches. The synchronizer operates with soft deadlines to avoid head-of-line blocking and is aware of kernel warm/cold states so it can trade a few ms of delay for large p99 reductions.
acceptance_criteria: p99 streaming latency reduced >= 30% for mixed synthetic traffic (short+long) on staging
p95 streaming latency reduced >= 15% for mixed synthetic traffic on staging
median latency increase <= 5ms for baseline text-generation workloads
no regression on throughput for long-sequence-only workloads (<5% throughput loss)
end-to-end canary shows no user-facing errors after 48h and meets SLOs
feature flags and config knobs available in runtime and console for tuning
design_notes:
Architecture: introduce a lightweight stage in the entry pipeline (Stream Synchronizer) that groups incoming tokens into micro-windows (configurable 2-10ms slack). A downstream Attention Slice Regulator uses a compact heuristic model (sequence-length prior + KV occupancy + entropy estimate) to decide whether to pre-warm attention buffers and hint preferred kernel variants to the kernel chooser.

Key decisions so far:
- Use soft micro-windows (non-blocking, timebox) rather than strict queueing to avoid added tail for high-priority requests.
- Keep the attention predictor deliberately cheap (linear features + small histogram-based lookup) to ensure it doesn't become a CPU bottleneck.
- Expose two knobs: micro_window_ms and attention_warm_threshold to ops via config store.

Trade-offs: micro-windows introduce small added latency for some short requests but increase kernel reuse and reduce p99 exponentially in simulations. More aggressive pre-warming increases memory pressure; regulator ensures pre-warm only when KV occupancy < threshold.

Related artifacts: design doc: https://company.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/STREAM-SYNC-DOC, prototype notebook: https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-proto-stream-sync
decisions: Soft timeboxed micro-windows (configurable) instead of strict batching
Cheap attention predictor instead of neural model to keep CPU overhead low
Expose tuning knobs via runtime config and Redwood Console
Prioritize kernel affinity for 2 subsequent micro-windows to favor reuse
implementation_plan: 1) Add Stream Synchronizer stage with micro-window queue and metrics
2) Implement Attention Slice Regulator and integrate with kernel chooser interface
3) Add config flags and guardrails (max_pre_warms_per_gpu, attention_warm_threshold)
4) Unit + integration tests for synchronizer and regulator logic
5) End-to-end benchmarking harness (mixed short+long synthetic traffic)
6) Canary rollout with 5% traffic, monitor p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit-rate, and memory usage
7) Iterate tuning knobs based on canary telemetry and roll to 25% then 100%
testing_plan: Unit tests for micro-window timer boundaries and non-blocking behavior
Fuzz tests: random short/long interleavings to ensure no deadlocks
Staging perf: run mixed workload generator (80% short 20% long; short seq=8-16 tokens; long seq=256-1024 tokens) for 6h
Compare kernel-switch counts per stream before/after; target >40% reduction in kernel handoffs for mixed traffic
Run memory pressure scenarios to validate pre-warm backoff behavior
Chaos test: kill one worker mid-micro-window to validate graceful cancellation and no resource leaks
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag: runtime.stream_synchronizer.enabled
Canary 1 (5%): enable on a single region (us-west-2) for non-enterprise tier; monitor for 48h
Canary 2 (25%): expand to two regions and enable attention pre-warm hints at low threshold
Full (100%): after 72h of stable telemetry and signoff from SRE
Rollback: revert flag or set micro_window_ms=0 immediately if p99 increases by >10% or error rate increases
comments: 2026-03-01 Aisha Patel: Triage — observed p99 spikes in prod traces during Tuesday afternoon burst; opened spike investigation. Hypothesis: frequent kernel handoffs + cold attention prefetch.
2026-03-03 Marco Ruiz: Architecture review — proposed micro-window coalescer + attention heuristic. Will prototype small simulator to measure kernel affinity impact.
2026-03-06 Marco Ruiz: Prototype results — synthetic sim shows 45% fewer kernel handoffs and 28% p99 reduction when micro_window_ms=6ms for mixed workload. CPU overhead ~0.8%.
2026-03-08 Elena Kim (SRE): Sizing note — pre-warm increases transient GPU memory by ~18MB per active pre-warm; recommended max_pre_warms_per_gpu=16 as safe default.
